CORPORATE OPPORTUNITY DOCTRINE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Widgets, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — CORPORATE OPPORTUNITY DOCTRINE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme Widgets, Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of California, and to Jordan Lee, who serves or served Acme Widgets, Inc. as its director and chief operating officer. It describes the corporate opportunity doctrine as California courts have stated it — the rule that a person who occupies a fiduciary relationship to a corporation may not acquire for that person's own benefit, in opposition to the corporation, a business opportunity in which the corporation has an interest or expectancy — including the tests courts use to identify a corporate opportunity, the factors that bear on whether a fiduciary was free to take an opportunity personally, the rule that these questions are primarily factual, the treatment of a director's purchase of the corporation's own shares in Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, the remedy of requiring the fiduciary to account to the corporation for the benefits obtained, and the parallel statutory duty to account for the appropriation of an entity opportunity that the Corporations Code states for members and managers of limited liability companies, general partners, and general partners of limited partnerships. Opportunity or transaction this information sheet may relate to, if applicable: purchase of the adjacent parcel the company had been negotiating to lease. Line of business of Acme Widgets, Inc., as described by the person completing this sheet: commercial real estate leasing and management.

This information sheet is about the appropriation of business opportunities by corporate fiduciaries. It is distinct from several other documents in this project: the Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions document, which covers the approval procedures of Corporations Code § 310 for contracts between a corporation and its own directors or officers; the Director's Duty of Care and the Business Judgment Rule document, which covers the standard of conduct Corporations Code § 309 sets for directors generally; the Controlling Shareholder Fiduciary Duty to Minority Shareholders document, which covers the duty of majority shareholders as such; the Shareholder Derivative Lawsuit document, which covers the procedural conditions Corporations Code § 800 places on suits brought in the corporation's right; and the LLC Member and Manager Fiduciary Duties and General Partner Fiduciary Duties in a California Limited Partnership documents, which cover the statutory duties of Corporations Code §§ 17704.09 and 15904.08 in full.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a complaint, a demand, a board resolution, a waiver, or any other filing or corporate act; does not determine whether any particular opportunity was a corporate opportunity of Acme Widgets, Inc., whether Jordan Lee or anyone else breached a duty described below, or what remedy, if any, a court would order; and does not constitute legal advice.

THE DOCTRINE: A CORPORATE FIDUCIARY MAY NOT ACQUIRE, IN OPPOSITION TO THE CORPORATION, PROPERTY IN WHICH THE CORPORATION HAS AN INTEREST OR TANGIBLE EXPECTANCY
The corporate opportunity doctrine is a branch of the duty of loyalty that directors, officers, and others in a fiduciary relationship to a corporation owe to it. The Court of Appeal in Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982 stated the doctrine by adopting the formulation of the Fletcher Cyclopedia of Corporations: the law has long recognized a doctrine that prohibits one who occupies a fiduciary relationship to a corporation from acquiring, in opposition to the corporation, property in which the corporation has an interest or tangible expectancy or which is essential to its existence. The same decision confirmed that California recognizes the doctrine, citing Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, and that whether a corporate opportunity exists is primarily a question of fact. Thompson v. Price, in turn, stated the rule by reproducing a passage from New v. New (1957) 148 Cal.App.2d 372, which itself quoted Industrial Indemnity Co. v. Golden State Co. (1953) 117 Cal.App.2d 519: since the Delaware decision in Guth v. Loft, it has been generally accepted that a corporate officer or director may not seize for himself, to the detriment of his company, business opportunities in the company's line of activities which the company has an interest and prior claim to obtain, and that if he seizes them in violation of his fiduciary duty the corporation may claim for itself all benefits so obtained.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The law has long recognized the doctrine of corporate opportunity which prohibits one who occupies a fiduciary relationship to a corporation from acquiring, in opposition to the corporation, property in which the corporation has an interest or tangible expectancy or which is essential to its existence."
  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 988 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  "California recognizes this doctrine and also recognizes that whether or not a corporate opportunity exists is primarily a factual question."
  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 989 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  "The rule regarding corporate opportunities is stated in New v. New, 148 Cal.App.2d 372, 384-385 [306 P.2d 987], quoting Industrial Indem. Co. v. Golden State Co., 117 Cal.App.2d 519, 533 [256 P.2d 677]"
  — Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 189 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214462/thompson-v-price/)
  "it has been generally accepted that a corporate officer or director may not seize for himself to the detriment of his company business opportunities in the company’s line of activities which the company has an interest and prior claim to obtain, and that if he seizes them in violation of his fiduciary duty the corporation may claim for itself all benefits so obtained by him."
  — Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 190 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214462/thompson-v-price/)
  Known gap: The Kelegian formulation is the court's quotation of a treatise (3 Fletcher Cyclopedia Corporations (1994 rev.) § 861.10), adopted as an accurate statement of the doctrine rather than announced as a rule of the court's own; the Thompson formulation is likewise a chain of quotations (Thompson quoting New v. New quoting Industrial Indemnity, which in turn quoted secondary authorities) and is reproduced here as it appears in Thompson. New v. New and Industrial Indemnity were not separately fetched for this document. In CourtListener's text of Thompson the introductory words of the quoted passage read "Since the leading ease of Guth v. Loft" (an apparent scanning artifact for "case"); the quotation below begins after those words. The doctrine described here is judge-made; no provision of the General Corporation Law defines a "corporate opportunity" for corporations, in contrast to the statutory language for other entity types described later in this document. This document does not determine whether any specific opportunity was one in which Acme Widgets, Inc. had an interest or expectancy.

IDENTIFYING A CORPORATE OPPORTUNITY: THE LINE-OF-BUSINESS, INTEREST-OR-EXPECTANCY, AND FAIRNESS TESTS
Kelegian, again drawing on the Fletcher treatise, described three tests that courts have recognized as standards for identifying a corporate opportunity: the "line of business" test, the "interest or expectancy" test, and the "fairness" test. The court stated that under any of the three tests, a corporate opportunity exists when a proposed activity is reasonably incident to the corporation's present or prospective business and is one in which the corporation has the capacity to engage. Whether a given opportunity bears the requisite relationship to the corporation is, in the passage the court adopted, largely a question of fact determined from the objective facts and surrounding circumstances existing at the time the opportunity arises, and whether an officer has misappropriated a corporate opportunity does not depend on any single factor. The Thompson v. Price formulation reflects the line-of-business strand of the doctrine, speaking of business opportunities in the company's "line of activities" which the company has an interest and prior claim to obtain.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Three tests have been recognized as standards for identifying a corporate opportunity"
  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 988 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  "Under any test, a corporate opportunity exists when a proposed activity is reasonably incident to the corporation’s present or prospective business and is one in which the corporation has the capacity to engage."
  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 988 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  "Whether or not an officer has misappropriated a corporate opportunity does not depend on any single factor."
  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 989 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  Known gap: The three tests are named in the treatise passage Kelegian quoted; the decision did not itself elaborate the line-of-business or fairness tests, and it applied the interest-or-expectancy test, which it described as the closest to the appellants' argument in that case. In CourtListener's text of Kelegian the name of the first test appears as "the Tine of business’ test" (an apparent scanning artifact for "the ‘line of business’ test"); the first quotation below is therefore cut before the names of the tests, which are stated in the body from the same passage. The sentence beginning "Whether or not a given opportunity meets" spans a reporter page break (988-989) in the fetched text and is paraphrased rather than quoted. This document does not determine which test a court would apply to any particular set of facts.

THE INTEREST-OR-EXPECTANCY TEST: A "BEACHHEAD," INTERFERENCE WITH CORPORATE PLANS, AND THE CORPORATION'S FINANCIAL RESOURCES
Kelegian applied the interest-or-expectancy test and, quoting the Fletcher treatise, described it as precluding the acquisition by corporate officers of the property of a business opportunity in which the corporation has a "beachhead," in the sense of a legal or equitable interest or expectancy growing out of a preexisting right or relationship. The same passage identifies the considerations courts weigh in deciding whether an officer may take advantage of a business opportunity in which a corporation is interested: whether the corporation had an interest, actual or expectancy, in the opportunity; whether the acquisition by the officer would hinder or defeat plans of the corporation in carrying on or developing the legitimate business for which it was created; and, in addition, whether the corporation has the financial resources to take advantage of the particular opportunity. Thompson v. Price similarly stated, in the passage it reproduced from the earlier decisions, that the question whether directors' and officers' duty of loyalty requires them to offer a particular opportunity discovered in connection with the corporate business to the corporation turns upon various factors as to the needs and situation of the corporation, its financial ability, and its fair expectation under the circumstances, which cannot be reduced to definite rules.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The ‘interest or expectancy’ test precludes acquisition by corporate officers of the property of a business opportunity in which the corporation has a ‘beachhead’ in the sense of a legal or equitable interest or expectancy growing out of a preexisting right or relationship."
  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 990 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  "In determining whether an officer may take advantage of a business opportunity in which a corporation is interested, courts consider whether the corporation had an interest, actual or expectancy, in the opportunity, and whether the acquisition by the officer would hinder or defeat plans of the corporation in carrying on or developing legitimate business for which it was created. In addition the courts may also consider whether the corporation has the financial resources to take advantage of a particular business opportunity."
  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 990 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  "The question is indeed often a close one whether the fiduciary duty of loyalty of directors and officers requires them to offer a particular business opportunity which they discover in connection with the corporate business to the corporation ... or whether they may take it for themselves. This turns . . . upon various factors as to the needs and situation of the corporation, its financial ability and fair expectation under the circumstances, which cannot be reduced to definite rules."
  — Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 190 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214462/thompson-v-price/)
  Known gap: The factors listed are drawn from the treatise passage Kelegian quoted (3 Fletcher Cyclopedia Corporations (1994 rev.) § 861.30) and from secondary authorities reproduced in Thompson; neither decision purports to make any one factor decisive, and Kelegian expressly stated that misappropriation does not depend on any single factor. The Thompson passage contains ellipses in the source ("to the corporation ... or whether" and "This turns . . . upon"), which are reproduced as they appear. Whether a corporation's lack of financial ability to pursue an opportunity excuses a fiduciary's taking it is a question on which the fetched decisions state only that courts "may also consider" the corporation's resources; this document does not determine how that consideration would apply to Acme Widgets, Inc.

A FAIRNESS STANDARD APPLIED TO PARTICULAR FACTS, DECIDED MAINLY BY THE TRIER OF FACT
The passage Thompson v. Price reproduced from New v. New and Industrial Indemnity locates the basis of the doctrine in the unfairness, on the particular facts, of a fiduciary taking advantage of an opportunity when the interests of the corporation justly call for protection, and describes the inquiry as calling for the application of ethical standards of what is fair and equitable to particular sets of facts. Because the decision in each case depends on its particular facts, the passage states that citation of examples is not useful, and that the determination of the factual circumstances under which a fiduciary takes business opportunities for himself, and the application of the ethical standards of fairness and good faith required from a fiduciary to those facts, is mainly for the trier of the facts. Consistently with that allocation, Kelegian treated the appeal before it as "simply a substantial evidence case" and reviewed the trial court's finding that no corporate opportunity existed under the substantial evidence standard.

  — Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 190 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214462/thompson-v-price/)
  "Under these circumstances the decision in each case depends on its particular facts and citation of examples is not useful. The determination of the particular factual circumstances under which a fiduciary takes business opportunities for himself and the application of the ethical standards of fairness and good faith required from a fiduciary to said set of facts is mainly for the trier of the facts."
  — Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 190 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214462/thompson-v-price/)

  — Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 33 Cal.App.4th 982, 990 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263940/kelegian-v-mgrdichian/)
  Known gap: Statements that an issue is "mainly for the trier of the facts" and that appellate review is for substantial evidence describe how the question is decided and reviewed, not what the outcome will be in any given case. The Thompson passage attributes the fairness formulation to Ballantine on Corporations and other secondary sources, which were not fetched. Kelegian's "substantial evidence" characterization was made in affirming a judgment for the defendants; the decision also noted that the trial court had considered the case a close one. This document does not predict how a trier of fact would resolve any dispute concerning Acme Widgets, Inc.

WHAT THE DOCTRINE DOES NOT REACH: A FIDUCIARY'S OWN BUSINESS ACTIVITY IN THE SAME FIELD, SHORT OF COMPETING TO THE CORPORATION'S DETRIMENT
The rule as reproduced in Thompson v. Price is expressly qualified: the doctrine does not exclude the fiduciary from all business activity of his own in the field in which he works for others. The same passage adds the limit that the directors or officers of a going, solvent corporation cannot engage in a competing business to the detriment of the corporation which they represent. Thompson applied the qualification on its facts. There, an attorney who was also a director and officer of a small real estate investment corporation had profited personally from real estate investments made while he held those positions; the trial court declined to order an accounting, and the Court of Appeal affirmed that part of the judgment, holding that evidence of the other shareholder's unwillingness to invest in raw acreage other than the corporation's one property, of the corporation's investment capital ratio, and of the nature of the corporation as an investment tool not intended to restrict its shareholders' personal investments sufficiently supported the finding that the director had not profited through usurping corporate opportunities.

  "The directors or officers of a going, solvent corporation cannot, however, engage in a competing business to the detriment of the corporation which they represent."
  — Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 251 Cal.App.2d 182, 190 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2214462/thompson-v-price/)

The sentence describing that evidence spans a reporter page break (190-191) in the fetched text; the quotation below begins after the break. The phrase "going, solvent corporation" comes from a secondary source (13 Am.Jur. 953, Corporations, § 999) quoted within the reproduced passage. This document does not determine whether any activity of Jordan Lee falls within the permitted category or constitutes competition to the detriment of Acme Widgets, Inc.

APPLICATION IN KELEGIAN: A DIRECTOR'S PURCHASE OF THE CORPORATION'S OWN SHARES IS NOT A CORPORATE OPPORTUNITY ABSENT A CORPORATE POLICY OR FORMAL ACTION
Kelegian v. Mgrdichian involved a derivative action brought on behalf of a closely held card-club corporation by several of its shareholders, who contended that a director's purchase of 200 shares from a fellow director should be voided as the misappropriation of a corporate opportunity, on the theory that the corporation had a longstanding objective of maintaining proportionate ownership and repurchasing its own shares. The Court of Appeal observed that no California authority had addressed the doctrine in the context of a director's purchase of corporate shares, and adopted the approach of an Oregon decision, Zidell v. Zidell (1977) 277 Ore. 560, under which a director ordinarily violates no duty by dealing in the corporation's stock on his own account, and, absent a corporate policy of purchasing its own stock, there is normally no special corporate interest in the opportunity to purchase its own shares. The court rejected the appellants' position that, as a matter of law, whenever directors speak of potentially purchasing shares on behalf of the corporation the purchasing director is on notice of a corporate opportunity. Although some directors had voiced concerns about proportionality, there was no formal corporate action on which a court could base a finding of a "beachhead" establishing a corporate opportunity; the corporation's only documented share-repurchase effort (to reduce its shareholder count and regain S corporation status) had been completed weeks before the purchase in question, and no other director had expressed interest in buying the shares. The court held that the record supported the trial court's finding that the parties' actions belied any corporate interest or intent to repurchase the shares for the corporation's benefit.

The Zidell language quoted below is Kelegian's own quotation of the Oregon opinion, which was not separately fetched. The trial court in Kelegian also relied on laches, which the Court of Appeal found unnecessary to address. The two CourtListener text representations of Kelegian disagree on the surname of the director who sold the shares (the opinion's HTML text renders it "Stem", the search-index text "Stern"); the quotations below are cut so as not to include the name, and the body refers to that person as a fellow director. This document does not determine whether Acme Widgets, Inc. has any policy or has taken any action that would give it an interest in acquiring its own shares.

THE REMEDY: THE CORPORATION MAY CLAIM THE BENEFITS THE FIDUCIARY OBTAINED
The rule as stated in Thompson v. Price carries its own remedy: if a corporate officer or director seizes a corporate opportunity in violation of his fiduciary duty, the corporation may claim for itself all benefits so obtained by him. The procedural vehicle in Thompson was a claim that the director account to the corporation for profits made in transactions he entered into while an officer, director, and attorney for the corporation, and in Kelegian it was a derivative claim, brought on the corporation's behalf, to void the director's purchase of shares. Because the claim belongs to the corporation, a shareholder who sues to enforce it ordinarily does so derivatively, subject to the conditions on such suits described in this project's Shareholder Derivative Lawsuit document. Thompson also illustrates a related equitable remedy available against a faithless fiduciary: the court directed the imposition of a constructive trust on the stock the director and his wife held in the corporation, on the ground that, having taken no financial risk while drawing more from the corporation than they had contributed, they would be unjustly enriched if allowed to retain an interest in it.

STATUTORY COUNTERPARTS: THE DUTY TO ACCOUNT FOR THE APPROPRIATION OF AN LLC, PARTNERSHIP, OR LIMITED PARTNERSHIP OPPORTUNITY
For unincorporated entities, the Corporations Code states the opportunity rule expressly as part of a codified duty of loyalty. Under the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member of a member-managed limited liability company owes the company and the other members a duty of loyalty that includes accounting to the company, and holding as trustee for it, any property, profit, or benefit derived by the member in the conduct and winding up of the company's activities or derived from a use by the member of company property, "including the appropriation of a limited liability company opportunity" (Corp. Code § 17704.09(b)(1)); in a manager-managed company that duty applies to the managers rather than the members, and a member has no fiduciary duty to the company or other members solely by reason of being a member (§ 17704.09(f)). The Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 imposes the same duty on each partner of a general partnership, extending it to benefits derived from the use of partnership property "or information, including the appropriation of a partnership opportunity" (§ 16404(b)(1)), and the Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 imposes it on the general partner of a limited partnership (§ 15904.08(b)(1)). Each of these statutes also provides that the fiduciary does not violate a duty merely because the fiduciary's conduct furthers the fiduciary's own interest.

STATUTORY BACKDROP FOR CORPORATE DIRECTORS: THE GENERAL STANDARD OF CONDUCT IN CORPORATIONS CODE § 309
For corporations, the General Corporation Law contains no provision naming corporate opportunities, but it does state the general standard against which a director's conduct is measured. Corporations Code § 309(a) requires a director to perform the duties of a director in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders, and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances. The corporate opportunity doctrine is a branch of the duty of loyalty that directors, officers, and others in a fiduciary relationship to a corporation owe to it. The Court of Appeal in Kelegian v. Mgrdichian (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 982 stated the doctrine by adopting the formulation of the Fletcher Cyclopedia of Corporations: the law has long recognized a doctrine that prohibits one who occupies a fiduciary relationship to a corporation from acquiring, in opposition to the corporation, property in which the corporation has an interest or tangible expectancy or which is essential to its existence. The same decision confirmed that California recognizes the doctrine, citing Thompson v. Price (1967) 251 Cal.App.2d 182, and that whether a corporate opportunity exists is primarily a question of fact. Thompson v. Price, in turn, stated the rule by reproducing a passage from New v. New (1957) 148 Cal.App.2d 372, which itself quoted Industrial Indemnity Co. v. Golden State Co. (1953) 117 Cal.App.2d 519: since the Delaware decision in Guth v. Loft, it has been generally accepted that a corporate officer or director may not seize for himself, to the detriment of his company, business opportunities in the company's line of activities which the company has an interest and prior claim to obtain, and that if he seizes them in violation of his fiduciary duty the corporation may claim for itself all benefits so obtained.

The rule regarding corporate opportunities is stated in New v. New, 148 Cal.App.2d 372, 384-385 [306 P.2d 987], quoting Industrial Indem. Co. v. Golden State Co., 117 Cal.App.2d 519, 533 [256 P.2d 677]

Mgrdichian involved a derivative action brought on behalf of a closely held card-club corporation by several of its shareholders, who contended that a director's purchase of 200 shares from a fellow director should be voided as the misappropriation of a corporate opportunity, on the theory that the corporation had a longstanding objective of maintaining proportionate ownership and repurchasing its own shares. The Court of Appeal observed that no California authority had addressed the doctrine in the context of a director's purchase of corporate shares, and adopted the approach of an Oregon decision, Zidell v. Zidell (1977) 277 Ore. 560, under which a director ordinarily violates no duty by dealing in the corporation's stock on his own account, and, absent a corporate policy of purchasing its own stock, there is normally no special corporate interest in the opportunity to purchase its own shares. The court rejected the appellants' position that, as a matter of law, whenever directors speak of potentially purchasing shares on behalf of the corporation the purchasing director is on notice of a corporate opportunity. Although some directors had voiced concerns about proportionality, there was no formal corporate action on which a court could base a finding of a "beachhead" establishing a corporate opportunity; the corporation's only documented share-repurchase effort (to reduce its shareholder count and regain S corporation status) had been completed weeks before the purchase in question, and no other director had expressed interest in buying the shares. The court held that the record supported the trial court's finding that the parties' actions belied any corporate interest or intent to repurchase the shares for the corporation's benefit.

expectedJSON.body: The rule as stated in Thompson v. Price carries its own remedy: if a corporate officer or director seizes a corporate opportunity in violation of his fiduciary duty, the corporation may claim for itself all benefits so obtained by him. The procedural vehicle in Thompson was a claim that the director account to the corporation for profits made in transactions he entered into while an officer, director, and attorney for the corporation, and in Kelegian it was a derivative claim, brought on the corporation's behalf, to void the director's purchase of shares. Because the claim belongs to the corporation, a shareholder who sues to enforce it ordinarily does so derivatively, subject to the conditions on such suits described in this project's Shareholder Derivative Lawsuit document. Thompson also illustrates a related equitable remedy available against a faithless fiduciary: the court directed the imposition of a constructive trust on the stock the director and his wife held in the corporation, on the ground that, having taken no financial risk while drawing more from the corporation than they had contributed, they would be unjustly enriched if allowed to retain an interest in it.

expectedJSON.body: For unincorporated entities, the Corporations Code states the opportunity rule expressly as part of a codified duty of loyalty. Under the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member of a member-managed limited liability company owes the company and the other members a duty of loyalty that includes accounting to the company, and holding as trustee for it, any property, profit, or benefit derived by the member in the conduct and winding up of the company's activities or derived from a use by the member of company property, "including the appropriation of a limited liability company opportunity" (Corp. Code § 17704.09(b)(1)); in a manager-managed company that duty applies to the managers rather than the members, and a member has no fiduciary duty to the company or other members solely by reason of being a member (§ 17704.09(f)). The Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 imposes the same duty on each partner of a general partnership, extending it to benefits derived from the use of partnership property "or information, including the appropriation of a partnership opportunity" (§ 16404(b)(1)), and the Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 imposes it on the general partner of a limited partnership (§ 15904.08(b)(1)). Each of these statutes also provides that the fiduciary does not violate a duty merely because the fiduciary's conduct furthers the fiduciary's own interest.
